Change Status: `planned`
Owner: Engineering

Last verified: {{generated_at}}

## Rationale

Why this change is needed. State a specific motivation a reviewer can understand without additional context.

## Product Intent

State who benefits, the observable before/after outcome, and material boundaries. One sentence can suffice, including for framework, maintenance and documentation work. Describe the outcome rather than prescribing a mechanism; link relevant behavior contracts when useful.

## Requirements

## Scope

**Problem statement:** [What is broken, missing, or improving?]

**In scope:**

- …

**Out of scope:**

- …

## Acceptance Criteria

Name at least one AC, or a clearly identified combination, that tests whether the intent was established. Keep implementation checks where useful; delivery of guidance alone does not prove improved agent behavior.

- [ ] AC-1: [Testable outcome]

## Tasks

- [ ] [Concrete implementation step]

## Agent Execution Graph

For a simple sequence, use a list. If work branches or rejoins, you may add a fenced `mermaid` flowchart here and name every prerequisite for the join in a sentence. Put dependencies between specs in the wave record and keep its `Depends On:` entries. See Plan spec for supported diagram syntax.

| Workstream | Owner | Depends On | Notes |

| [workstream] | [role] | — | |

## Serialization Points

(Replace this note with review targets. These examples are fenced so the scaffold declares nothing.)

```
- `src/app/handler.py`, `docs/specs/`
```

When a target contains a space, use an explicit block; keep examples fenced:

```
**Review targets (repo-relative paths):**

- `docs/waves/1abc some slug/wave.md`
```

Prepare selects automatic review lanes from declared paths, not from narrative prose. Any example retained in this template must remain fenced. Verify this scaffold declares no targets before use.

A declared path token has at least one `/`, so a root-level file (a changelog, a readme) is never a token in either form, and a bullet declares all or nothing in either form, so one such token turns the whole bullet into prose and every other path in it goes undeclared with it. In a bullet a `*` disqualifies the token too; inside the explicit block a span is kept only when its last segment carries an extension or the span ends in `/`, so there a `*` span is accepted as a phantom (a `*.json`, a `dir/*/`) that matches no file and recruits a lane only through a trigger token it happens to carry (a directory prefix, an extension, or a trigger basename), a block holding only phantoms leaves the document declared with whatever roster those triggers recruit (empty when none is a trigger), and any other `*` span turns its bullet into prose. Put a root-level file in its own prose bullet, and declare the directory that holds globbed files.

# Implement Wave

Owner: Engineering
Status: active
Last verified: {{generated_at}}

Shortcut: **`Implement wave`**

## Host-neutral orchestration

Follow `.wavefoundry/framework/seeds/180-implement-spec.prompt.md` **Host-neutral orchestration** across the lifecycle. Choose models and reasoning effort per implementation or verification task; accept changes only after coordinator integration checks. Use only available host capabilities; sequential implementation does not satisfy required independent review.

## Purpose

Open a readied wave and execute all admitted changes through a focused
implement and verify loop, then hand the completed evidence to `Review wave`.

## Readiness handoff

Before the first code edit, confirm `Prepare wave` completed and its current
typed readiness approval is recorded. Prepare owns the failure-first critique
and packet-completeness decision; implementation does not repeat that review.

**Readback before editing:**

Before the first implementation edit of each change, record a concise `Readback:` in its existing Progress Log and surface its substance to the operator: intended behavior, relevant ACs, important scope boundary, and expected affected files. Include one before/after example for nontrivial behavior changes; keep clear tasks brief. Briefly relate the chosen work to Product Intent (or the wave Objective); name how the mechanism serves the intended outcome. Intent does not authorize broader scope or silent contract changes: preserve existing requirement-amendment, re-Prepare and operator-authorization rules.

Correct an agent-only misreading directly from the established requirement. Route an actual contract contradiction or missing consequential decision back to planning under existing escalation rules, pausing only dependent work. A readback correction is not automatically Level 3 and adds no second approval. Refresh only materially changed understanding after scope changes or handoff; do not repeat an unchanged readback or create another artifact.

## Execution

1. Use repository-native navigation and the Wavefoundry code tools to identify
   ownership, callers, and established patterns before editing.
2. Implement only admitted scope and preserve unrelated working-tree changes.
3. Update AC and task checkboxes as evidence is produced. When one change
   finishes before the others, `wf_close_change(wave_id, change_id, mode)`
   closes it to `complete` (dry-run first) and moves the dependents whose
   `Depends On:` names it to `ready`; the wave stays open and `Close wave`
   remains the only wave close.
4. Run focused tests after each bounded repair and the canonical project suite
   before delivery review.
5. Record findings when discovered during an exceptional named checkpoint or
   the later delivery review, record `repair_start` before mutation,
   repair immediately, and reverify in the currently open partial repair cycle.
   Advancing a cycle number is chronology, not a reason to delay the repair or
   summon another council.
6. Re-prepare only when scope, required contracts, architecture ownership,
   trust boundaries, or readiness semantics materially change.
7. When a choice or discovery occurs, record in the affected spec what the next
   engineer needs that the diff and tests cannot reliably show. Follow seed
   180's **Rationale for the next engineer** for what belongs in
   `## Decision Log` and `## Progress Log`. A routine fix needs only its
   ordinary completion entry. Seed 180's **Retrospective on rationale records**
   sets the later review of this guidance.

## When the Wavefoundry MCP is attached

Before the first edit, call `memory_brief(context='pre_implementation', targets=[...])` for the files in scope. At completion, run full `wf_validate_docs` and resolve its findings. Delegate code work through a role-typed agent or carry the MCP-first navigation directive in the worker's prompt, checking its actual tools and allowlist.

Without MCP, follow the repository's documented navigation and validation fallbacks.

Follow seed 180's **Wave orchestration contract → Allocation** for implementation lane selection on every host.

`wf_implement_wave` checks and consumes current readiness authority; it does not call Prepare automatically. If readiness is missing or stale, follow the returned Prepare/review remedy before source edits.

## Completion

Keep routine briefings, per-seat reports, probe captures, source baselines and green logs in task context or the lifecycle-reported disposable work area. Consolidate final outcomes and evidence in the existing wave/change records under seed 209's Review Artifact Discipline; preserve cited and unique proof, explaining retained exceptions inline in `wave.md`.

Consume successful typed-write continuation actions and confirm current readiness/delivery authority without repeating unchanged review or list calls. Finish material verification-input edits before the canonical suite; validated routine ledger/projection updates and normalized progress/status/completion may continue under seed 209's Continuation And Qualification Discipline. Use Progress Log during a run; the standalone session handoff and other documentation outside the wave under test may also change during it, as seed 209 describes. Routine recording alone does not require another suite or reviewer cycle; reuse only a successful receipt matching current inputs. Required lanes, focused independent repair review and final full docs validation remain unchanged. An operator-authorized close uses one canonical mutation; dry-run resolves uncertain checks and is not a compulsory extra gate.

Implementation is complete only when the admitted behavior, docs, tests, and
review evidence agree. It does not authorize commit, release, or wave closure.

## Disposable work

Use the lifecycle-reported `.wavefoundry/work/<wave-id>/`, keyed by the resolved unique prefix, for shared temporary work; include the path and availability notices in coordinator briefs. Follow seed 180’s **Disposable work** and seed 209’s **Review Artifact Discipline**. Reads and dry-runs create nothing; unavailable work is advisory and existing host permissions apply.

Write every file you create for a wave, including coordinator briefs, logs, captured test output and build output, inside that wave's own work folder, in a child folder when that helps; never write a file directly in `.wavefoundry/work/`. Before the wave exists, keep the content in task context until a lifecycle call reports the work area. `wf_audit` and close report files and links left directly in the work root as the advisory `work_root_loose_files`. If you wrote such a file for a wave, move it into that wave's folder while the wave is open, or delete it. Leave any other loose file in place, including one you are not sure you wrote (a name that starts with a wave id does not prove who wrote it), and report it to the operator, who decides. Never move a file you did not write into a wave's folder: close removes that folder with everything in it.
lifecycle-prompts/memory-review.prompt.m:
# Review Memories

Owner: Engineering
Status: active
Last verified: 2026-08-02

Shortcut: **`Review memories`**
Alias: **`Memory review`**

Use this maintenance workflow when the operator asks to review, consolidate, archive,
or purge repository memory. Invocation is apply-oriented: it authorizes the reviewed,
eligible memory mutations below, including irreversible purge. If the operator explicitly
asks for a read-only review, use the separate read-only procedure and make no mutation.

## Safety boundaries

- Review meaning and current evidence; never retire a record because of age alone. The
  audit order selects a record for review and never decides its outcome.
- Treat the active-memory budget as a curation signal, not a deletion quota. Do not merge
  unrelated records or remove useful knowledge merely to reach the cap.
- Decisions, operator preferences, and fragile-file records are protected kinds. Supply
  `eligibility_confirmed=true` only after current review proves that protected knowledge is
  no longer operational.
- Leave unresolved judgment calls unchanged and report them.
- Archive only memories that remain important to project history. Git remains the recovery
  record for everything else, so purge reviewed retired records that are not history-worthy.
  The exception: records the active-record audit retires are archived in the same run, never
  purged in it, so a later review gives them a second look before any purge.

## Apply procedure

1. Inventory before-state counts and bytes. Use `memory_brief(context="review")`, then
   `memory_search(...)` and `memory_search(include_history=true, ...)` as needed to inspect
   active, candidate, retired, and archived records. Follow cited evidence and current targets.
2. Route candidates by provenance:
   - For an evidence-derived candidate containing both `Source event:` and
     `Validation: pending`, call
     `memory_validate(memory_id=..., verdict=..., action_delta=..., rationale=...,
     evidence_verified=..., current_target_verified=..., canonical_overlap=...,
     rewrite_kind=..., rewrite_title=..., rewrite_summary=..., rewrite_evidence=...,
     rewrite_targets=..., rewrite_confidence=...)`. Supply every `rewrite_*` value only when
     `verdict="rewrite"`.
   - Never send a hand-authored or already-finalized candidate to `memory_validate`. When
     justified, disposition it with `memory_reconcile(memory_id=...,
     status="active"|"rejected")`; otherwise leave it unchanged and report it unresolved.
3. Audit a bounded batch of active records. List it with
   `memory_search(status="active", order="least_recently_reviewed", limit=15)`: the 15 active
   records of every kind whose `updated_at` is oldest, weakest effective confidence first on a
   tie. Protected kinds retire only after current review proves the knowledge is no longer
   operational. Archive every record this step retires in step 6; do not purge it in this run.
   Record one outcome and a reason that names current evidence for each record:
   - **keep:** the record still changes a future action, or you cannot name the evidence another
     outcome needs. Stamp it with `memory_reconcile(memory_id=..., status="active")`, which
     rewrites only its `Updated:` line and moves it to the end of the order. The stamp means
     "reviewed, unchanged", not a content change. Repeated runs advance through the corpus.
   - **retire to stale, encoded elsewhere:** name the specific assertion (test, check or code
     path) that would fail on a regression of the lesson. It must cover the lesson's whole scope,
     not only the instance the record came from; otherwise keep or rewrite. Then call
     `memory_reconcile(memory_id=..., status="stale")`.
   - **retire to stale, target gone or duplicate:** name the missing target path, or the canonical
     document and section that already carries the same action.
   - **supersede:** another active record carries the knowledge at equal or wider scope. Call
     `memory_reconcile(memory_id=..., status="superseded", superseded_by=...)`.
   - **rewrite:** the knowledge is still operational but the record is wrong or outdated. Call
     `memory_add(..., status="active", supersedes=<original id>)`; it also marks the original
     superseded. Only when it reports `supersedes_target_not_updated`, finish with
     `memory_reconcile(memory_id=<original id>, status="superseded", superseded_by=<new id>)`.
     Never send an active record to `memory_validate`.
   - **unresolved:** leave the record unchanged and report it.
4. Call `memory_consolidate(mode="dry_run")`. If a related group is worth consolidating,
   apply at most one exact returned group with
   `memory_consolidate(mode="create", memory_ids=<one exact groups[].memory_ids>,
   title=..., summary=..., reviewed=true, eligibility_confirmed=...)`. Set
   `eligibility_confirmed=true` only after current protected-kind review. The tool does not
   expose or accept a bulk retired-record cleanup list; disposition retired records individually.
5. Consolidation creates the replacement before superseding and archiving every selected
   source. Verify the replacement through `memory_search(...)` and
   `memory_search(include_history=true, ...)`. Do not re-archive those source IDs. Retain a
   source archive only when it remains history-worthy; otherwise purge that retired source
   individually with `memory_purge(memory_id=..., reviewed=true,
   eligibility_confirmed=...)`.
6. Review retired records individually, both those retired before this run and those the
   audit retired in step 3:
   - Archive every record the audit retired in step 3 with `memory_reconcile(memory_id=...,
     status="archived", retain_for_history=true, archive_reason=..., eligibility_confirmed=...)`.
   - For a record retired before this run, keep important history with
     `memory_reconcile(memory_id=..., status="archived", retain_for_history=true,
     archive_reason=..., eligibility_confirmed=...)`.
   - For a record retired before this run, remove unimportant history with
     `memory_purge(memory_id=..., reviewed=true, eligibility_confirmed=...)`.
   Protected kinds receive `eligibility_confirmed=true` only after the current review.
7. Verify the final live and historical corpus with `memory_search(...)` and
   `memory_search(include_history=true, ...)`, then run `wf_validate_docs()`.
8. Run `index_build(content="docs", mode="update")`. If it reports `up_to_date=true`,
   continue. Otherwise poll `index_build_status(layer="project")` until `lock.held=false`,
   `lock.ended_at` records clean completion, and either `state="finished"` or
   `state="idle"` with `epoch.status="complete"` and `epoch.interrupted=false`. If the
   build fails, is interrupted, or never reaches one of those clean terminal forms,
   stop and report it; do not evaluate memory against a stale or partial index.
9. After clean index completion, run `index_health()` and `wf_memory_eval()`, then report.

## Read-only procedure

When the operator explicitly requests read-only review, use only:

- `memory_brief(context="review")`
- `memory_search(...)` and `memory_search(include_history=true, ...)`
- `memory_search(status="active", order="least_recently_reviewed", limit=15)` for the audit
  walk: report the batch and each proposed outcome with its reason
- `memory_consolidate(mode="dry_run")`
- `wf_memory_eval()`

Do not call `memory_validate`, consolidation create, `memory_reconcile`, `memory_add`,
`memory_purge`, any docs mutation, or any index mutation in the read-only procedure.

## Report

Keep the result compact and include:

- before/after counts by status, disposition counts, and active count versus budget;
- unresolved records left unchanged;
- active-record audit counts: audited, kept, retired, superseded, rewritten and unresolved,
  plus each retired or superseded record with its reason, protected kinds listed separately;
- live-corpus bytes before/after: UTF-8 byte sizes of lint-valid record bodies directly
  under `docs/agents/memory/`, excluding `README.md` and `archive/`;
- estimated removed tokens as `ceil(max(before_bytes - after_bytes, 0) / 4)`, clearly
  labeled as an estimate;
- archive-body file count and total UTF-8 bytes under `docs/agents/memory/archive/`, plus
  `docs/agents/memory-archive.md` bytes reported separately; and
- final docs validation, index health, and memory-evaluation results when available.

Do not record model names.

# Close Wave

Owner: Engineering
Status: active
Last verified: {{generated_at}}

Shortcut: **`Close wave`**

## Operator-selected small changes

On an eligible small change, close checks the current delivered contents against the independent code reviewer’s approval. Follow the returned review actions when the files have changed or the work has expanded. The operator still signs off and explicitly directs closure.

## Host-neutral orchestration

Follow `.wavefoundry/framework/seeds/180-implement-spec.prompt.md` **Host-neutral orchestration** across the lifecycle. Choose models and reasoning effort for reconciliation and unresolved judgments by task fit. Efficient routine checks do not waive review evidence or explicit operator closure authority. Use only available host capabilities; sequential implementation does not satisfy required independent review.

## Purpose

Close a delivered wave after implementation, review, documentation, and
handoff state are fully reconciled. Close wave is the only wave close, whatever
the change count.

## Close a paused delivery

When the operator authorizes closure, pass the ID of the paused delivery directly to Close. Keep the currently open wave’s handoff, focus and edit gates intact, including when Close refuses or retries. The reviewed delivery still goes through the ordinary close checks, including any required current test receipt.

## Closure checks

All closure-time code and docs investigation follows the run contract's
Retrieval Rules (`seed-020`): MCP retrieval tools first, for every lane and
briefed subagent.

1. Every change is `implemented`, `complete`, or `deferred` with rationale, and
   every AC and task is completed or intentionally deferred with rationale.
   **Close spec** (`wf_close_change`) is optional; use it to mark a single
   change `complete` and activate its dependents inside the open wave.
2. Required review lanes are current. Check each Council signoff required by the current Prepare receipt for its phase (`council-readiness` or `council-delivery`).
3. Change status, wave status, completion date, and chronology agree.
4. Architecture, behavior contracts, public prompts, and release notes reflect the
   delivered behavior.
5. Journals, durable memory candidates, and the session handoff are reconciled.
   Run `memory_propose(wave_id, mode='create')`, then use
   `memory_validate` on every evidence-derived candidate. The validating
   agent follows the linked evidence and current target, states the future
   action delta, checks canonical overlap and confidence, and records
   `promote`, `retain`, `reject`, or `rewrite`. A wave may correctly produce
   zero memories; a missing or pending eligible candidate blocks close.
6. The canonical test suite, docs gate, and relevant packaging checks pass.
7. The context-efficiency checkpoint has been projected from durable telemetry
   when telemetry is available.
8. Run `wf_close_wave(mode='dry_run')` before requesting operator approval.
9. Before the final docs validation and the close write, read the dry run's
   advisory `record_extras_present`, which lists each file in the wave folder
   other than the record, its admitted specs and its ledger, with size and
   citation state. Give every listed file one disposition: keep it and name it
   with the reason in `## Review Checkpoints`; summarize it there or in a
   spec's Progress Log, then remove it; or remove it. Always keep a
   `cited_in_ledger` file, a `cited_in_record` file whose citation sits in a
   spec section other than the Progress Log, and a `not_cited` file with
   `name_in_ledger`, `name_in_record` or `directory_in_ledger` true. Before
   removing a `not_cited` file with all four booleans false, search the ledger
   for its name stem and the other extras for its name; a match keeps it. When
   in doubt, keep it and say why. The report lists at most 50 files: list the
   folder yourself and give every extra a disposition under the same rules,
   including files the report does not list, and review the folder by hand
   when `complete` is false. An unlisted file has no citation state or flags,
   so search the ledger, the record and the specs for its path, name and
   directories, and keep it unless nothing refers to it. Follow seed 190's **Wave-folder cleanup** for the full rules;
   the tool removes nothing and blocks nothing.

Before closure, explicitly author one concise `Intent outcome:` paragraph in the existing exact `## Review Checkpoints` section: state achieved, partial or not established, cite evidence, and retain material limitations. When the plan states a measure of success, cite it and say whether it can be read yet. It may cover changes sharing an outcome. The close-summary composer carries the last such paragraph or list item (optionally dated `YYYY-MM-DD: `) into Wave Summary, preserving its text and qualification; do not infer achievement from titles or checked ACs. Legacy records without this assessment remain closable under existing gates and retain their existing summary behavior; this adds no schema or blocking gate. When the current `council-delivery` approval records `intent_fit: does_not`, Review and Close report the `delivery_intent_not_established` advisory; it does not block, and the operator's sign-off accepts that outcome.

Final review evaluates any reviewer/persona lanes newly applicable to the delivered scope. This is not a blanket rerun of an unchanged readiness Council. Material policy, roster or readiness changes follow existing re-Prepare and current-approval requirements; otherwise consume the current readiness authority and complete the required delivery reviews. A change admitted after delivery review makes the earlier delivery approvals not current once the wave is re-prepared, so re-Prepare, then record the affected delivery approvals again before closing.

## Operator authority

Only an explicit operator instruction authorizes `wf_close_wave(mode='create')`
or equivalent apply mode. Passing dry-run, finishing implementation, or asking
for review does not imply closure approval. Commit, tag, push, and release
authority remain separately operator-owned.

## Disposable work

Use the lifecycle-reported `.wavefoundry/work/<wave-id>/`, keyed by the resolved unique prefix, for shared temporary work; include the path and availability notices in coordinator briefs. Follow seed 180’s **Disposable work** and seed 209’s **Review Artifact Discipline**. Reads and dry-runs create nothing; unavailable work is advisory and existing host permissions apply. Before finalizing evidence, preserve unique long-term proof in maintained wave records, tests or explicitly retained evidence; new durable approvals must not rely solely on disposable paths. Only successful operator-authorized whole-wave closure attempts owned cleanup after its transition. Failure is advisory; unsupported safe deletion preserves files. Dry-run, failed close and single-change close preserve work. Authorized repeated close may retry; stale cleanup cannot remove a reopened generation. Ordinary wave-folder evidence is protected. Close reports, and never deletes, what it leaves: advisory `work_retained` when this record's folder stays (path, outcome `preserved` or `partially_removed`, reason, failed entry and errno, size and completeness, next action), `work_leftovers_present` for other folders of closed, archived or not-found records, `work_root_loose_files` for files and links left directly in the work root, and `work_path_cited` for maintained lines that cite this record's own work folder; `wf_audit` sizes the leftovers in `data.work_root`. To reclaim one such folder, preview `wf_cleanup_work(work_key='<key>')`, show the preview to the operator and call `mode='apply'` with its `confirmation` only when the operator directs cleanup of that key in the current request; native Windows previews and refuses apply.

Write every file you create for a wave, including coordinator briefs, logs, captured test output and build output, inside that wave's own work folder, in a child folder when that helps; never write a file directly in `.wavefoundry/work/`. Before the wave exists, keep the content in task context until a lifecycle call reports the work area. `wf_audit` and close report files and links left directly in the work root as the advisory `work_root_loose_files`. If you wrote such a file for a wave, move it into that wave's folder while the wave is open, or delete it. Leave any other loose file in place, including one you are not sure you wrote (a name that starts with a wave id does not prove who wrote it), and report it to the operator, who decides. Never move a file you did not write into a wave's folder: close removes that folder with everything in it.
lifecycle-prompts/close-change.prompt.md:
# Close Spec

Owner: Engineering
Status: active
Last verified: {{generated_at}}

Shortcut: **`Close spec`** | Alias: **`Close change`**

## Purpose

Close ONE admitted change inside an open wave with `wf_close_change`: mark it
`complete` and activate the dependents it unblocks. It works the same way
whether the wave has one change or many, and it never closes the wave.
**Close wave** remains the only wave close.

## When to run

Run Close spec only after **Review wave** has cleared the change. A completed
change cannot be reopened, and `wf_close_change` records no review evidence, so
closing a change does not satisfy or replace any review lane. Close spec is
optional: `wf_close_wave` accepts a change left `implemented`, so use it when a
change must be `complete` inside the open wave, for example to activate a
dependent change.

## Gates

For an operator-selected small change, the spec close checks the current review policy and the approved file contents. If the contents changed, obtain a fresh code-reviewer delivery approval. If the work moved to ordinary review, follow the listed approval requirements. Wave closure remains a separate operator decision.

First, before any gate and with nothing written, `wf_close_change` refuses
a wave record it cannot read unambiguously (`wave_record_ambiguous`): an id
in more than one record, a record with more than one status line (fenced or
not, readable or not), or a fenced example id line that starts a record.
Move fenced examples out of the record lines and retry.

`wf_close_change` reports every failing gate, in `dry_run` and `create`:

1. The wave is OPEN (`active` or `implementing`).
2. The change is admitted to that wave (pass the FULL change id).
3. Its spec exists and is readable.
4. Its status is closable (`ready`, `active`, `review` or `implemented`) and
   agrees between the wave record and the spec.
5. It has no silent `[ ]` AC or task; every item is `[x]` or `[~]` with a
   rationale.
6. Every dependency on its wave-record `Depends On:` line is done (terminal or
   `implemented`).

## Steps

1. Confirm Review wave has cleared the change.
2. Run `wf_close_change(wave_id, change_id)`; `dry_run` is the default and
   writes nothing. Fix every reported gate.
3. Run `wf_close_change(wave_id, change_id, mode='create')`. It writes
   `complete` into the spec and the wave record, and moves each
   `planned` or `blocked` dependent whose dependencies are now all done to
   `ready`.
4. After a successful close, count all admitted specs. If the selected spec
   is the sole member, you may offer **Close wave**. Wait for the operator's
   explicit approval before running it. With multiple admitted specs, leave
   the wave open even if the selected spec was its last unfinished member.
   **Close wave** handles all eligible members under its usual review and
   closure rules.

## Guardrails

- Never use Close spec to close a wave; **Close wave** is the only wave close.
- It writes no review evidence or ledger event and does not move the
  review-policy receipt.
- A completed change cannot be reopened, so never run it before Review wave
  has cleared the change.

# Explain

Owner: Engineering
Status: active
Last verified: {{generated_at}}

Shortcut: **`Explain`** or `/wf-explain`

Help the operator take responsibility for the changed code. Explain what the team built, how it works, why it took this shape and what still needs attention. Use the project's names for lifecycle records. Keep the walkthrough in the conversation.

## Choose the delivery

Use the delivery just reviewed when the engineer accepts the review offer. A direct request can name an open or closed record or a single admitted change. Ask which record they mean if the reference is ambiguous. Read the record, its decisions and review findings. Use `wf_get_change(wave_id=...)` for the admitted set or `wf_get_change(change_id=...)` for one change. Follow relevant code, documentation, diffs and verification records using the project's read-only retrieval tools. If a record is missing or work is unfinished, say which claims the available evidence supports.

On request, walk through a spec that is still in progress. Separate behavior that an executed check verified, work and checks that are still planned, and unknowns. Name each executed check with its result, and label a planned check as planned. A routine fix needs no walkthrough unless the operator asks for one.

## Walk through the change

- Start with one observable difference for a user or maintainer. For several changes, explain how they fit together and offer a place to drill down. For one named change, include a sibling only when a dependency explains the behavior.
- Trace a representative input or action through the real entry point to its result. Link to the relevant files and name the symbols. For a documentation or configuration change, trace the instruction or setting through to what the reader or system does.
- Use a diagram when it helps the maintainer follow a consequential request, state transition or recovery path. Keep a straightforward change in prose. Link a maintained architecture diagram if it accurately shows that path. If it is stale, identify the discrepancy and trace the path you verified.
- For a new diagram, name the components and give each arrow a verb that reads from source to target. Explain what crosses each boundary. Cite the entry point and the implementation or test supporting the trace, and say where the evidence ends. For a graphical walkthrough, follow **Dashboard flowchart syntax** in the project's planning prompt. Keep the diagram in the conversation and route permanent corrections through the project's documentation workflow.
- When the design changed, show where responsibility, data flow or a public contract moved. For a library added, replaced or removed, name it, locate its use and explain why the team chose it and what it requires of the maintainer. Check the diff and dependency manifest for the reviewed revision.
- If the implementation or its design record identifies a named algorithm, give its name, point to where it runs and explain what it does here. Explain why the algorithm works for this input and, separately, why the team picked it. Tie the selection to a recorded constraint, alternative or tradeoff. If the record explains only suitability, leave the selection rationale unknown. Leave unnamed logic in plain language.
- Tell the operator whether the team considered performance and security. For each, state the concern, the decision and any remaining exposure that the record supports. For a performance change, connect the old bottleneck to the implementation change and its effect on the user or operator. Give the before and after values, units, workload and comparison conditions when recorded. If the team measured only an intermediate metric such as queue operations, say what improved and whether it measured the resulting latency, cost or capacity. Label predictions as expectations. For security, distinguish a proposed safeguard from one the team exercised. If the diff shows a safeguard but the review gives no rationale, describe what the code does. If you find no recorded assessment, say so briefly. Silence establishes neither safety nor a performance result.
- Describe implementation problems that shaped the result, including ones the team resolved before review. Use the progress log, diff or finding to explain what failed, how the team handled it, and any cost or workaround the operator inherits. Skip routine debugging details.
- Explain a consequential choice and the alternative the team considered. Cite the decision, spec or finding that records the reason. If no one recorded a reason or alternative, say so. Identify any inference as your own.
- For each material claim, name the test, check or observation, its condition and the assertion that distinguishes success from failure. Identify what ran and its result. Match a historical result to the version of the check that ran. A stronger assertion in today's source or a green suite without that link leaves the stronger claim unverified. For example, counting failed accepts shows that the server retried. A fresh request succeeding on the same server shows that it recovered.
- Finish with the work the operator inherits: outstanding TODOs, temporary compromises, deferred checks or open decisions that affect this change. Say what will resolve each one and give its owner, issue or revisit condition when recorded. Separate resolved issues from remaining work and planned follow-ups from your own suggestions.
- Keep the handoff proportionate. Omit empty categories. When the operator asks about one, distinguish a verified absence from a gap in the record. Give the recorded reproduction command or next check when useful. Let the operator choose where to go deeper.

## Show the path in a terminal

In Codex CLI and Claude Code terminal sessions, draw the path directly in the reply in a fenced `text` block. Use the same default when the display is unknown. Put each verb on the arrow from its source to its target. For example, a handler reads a record and sends a reply:

```text
Handler
  +-- reads from --> Store
  +-- sends reply to --> Client
```

Keep lines short enough to read without wrapping. Stack steps vertically or split a wide graph into short paths. Repeat component names at joins and keep both verbs on parallel paths. Plain ASCII works when box-drawing characters display poorly. For zooming or sharing, link an existing SVG or dashboard view after the text diagram. If the reader requests a new SVG, handle the export separately from the read-only walkthrough.

## Test my understanding

Offer this optional exercise after the walkthrough, or start it on an explicit request. Ask **one** practical question about maintaining this delivery and end the turn. Choose a design decision, algorithm, dependency, performance or security tradeoff, workaround or open task with a real consequence. Wait for the engineer's answer. Use the actual assertion or decision to explain what their answer establishes and where it falls short. Let them retry, ask another question or stop. Accept a stop immediately. Keep answers and feedback unscored.

Use read-only operations throughout. A walkthrough, a declined or unanswered offer, and a teach-back have no effect on approvals, checklists or closure. Leave files and review events alone. If the conversation reveals a discrepancy, cite the evidence and point the engineer to the normal review or repair workflow.
